part.distant.title: Distant opposition
part.distant.summary: After your move, leave an odd number of squares between the kings: the opposition is yours. The king goes ahead with it; the pawn advances later.
part.lateral.title: Lateral opposition
part.lateral.summary: On the same rank the count is the same: an odd number of squares between the kings, after your move, leaves the opposition with you.
part.capablanca.title: Capablanca's example
part.capablanca.summary: The side to move leaves an odd number of squares between the kings; if the other king changes file, wait and take the opposition back before moving up.
part.edge.title: Lateral approach
part.edge.summary: Going straight for the pawn can hand over the opposition. Step away: the other king cannot use the squares your pawns watch.
ex.e09: Play White and find the best move. Your king starts in the corner, far from the d2-pawn. Find the first two king moves against the reply shown, preparing the approach through opposition.
ex.e09.hint:
First the black king's file, from afar. Then, every time he moves, shorten the distance facing him.

These do not work either:

At move 1
The king is still in the corner: advancing the pawn before bringing the king out lets the defender occupy the centre.
If White played 1.d3?, Black would reply 1...Kf7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.d3 Kf7 2.d4 Ke6.
If White played 1.d4?, Black would reply 1...Kf7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.d4 Kf7 2.d5 Kf6.

At move 2
The approach must shorten the distance; staying back on the second rank lets the black king establish its defence.
If White played 2.Kf2?, Black would reply 2...Ke6 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Kf2 Ke6 3.d3 Kd5.
ex.e09.solution:
1.Kg2! takes distant opposition on the g-file, with five squares between the kings. After 1...Kf7, 2.Kf3! maintains opposition on the f-file, now with three intervening squares. The exercise ends here: you have prepared the approach and preserved the win, but a game would still require conversion.

A continuation using the technique studied shows how to reduce the distance: 2...Ke6 3.Ke4 Kd6 4.Kd4. The kings reach direct opposition beside the pawn. If White started with the pawn or with another king move, Black would draw.

These do not work either:

At move 1: The king is still in the corner: advancing the pawn before bringing the king out lets the defender occupy the centre. If White played 1.d3?, Black would reply 1...Kf7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.d3 Kf7 2.d4 Ke6. If White played 1.d4?, Black would reply 1...Kf7 and hold the draw. The line would be 1.d4 Kf7 2.d5 Kf6.

At move 2: The approach must shorten the distance; staying back on the second rank lets the black king establish its defence. If White played 2.Kf2?, Black would reply 2...Ke6 and hold the draw. The line would be 2.Kf2 Ke6 3.d3 Kd5.
ex.e11: Play Black and find the best move. The white pawn is still on the second rank, and your king must stop the white king from reaching the key squares. Keep up the defence through the replies shown, adjusting the opposition when the opponent changes file.
ex.e11.hint:
Choose the distance that keeps the opposing king away from the key squares. Defence sometimes requires a retreat; after the opponent approaches, it may require shortening the distance. Recheck the kings’ alignment and whose turn it will be after each reply.

These do not work either:

At move 1
Distant opposition must be obtained on the white king’s file, at the correct distance; a difference of one file or rank opens the approach.
If Black played 1...Ke8?, White would reply 2.Kd2 and win. The line would be 1...Ke8 2.Kd2 Kd7 3.Kc3.
If Black played 1...Kf7?, White would reply 2.Kd2 and win. The line would be 1...Kf7 2.Kd2 Ke6 3.Kc3.

At move 2
After the change of file, the defence must shorten the distance on the correct axis.
If Black played 2...Kd7?, White would reply 3.Kc3 and win. The line would be 2...Kd7 3.Kc3 Kd6 4.Kc4.
If Black played 2...Ke6?, White would reply 3.Kc3 and win. The line would be 2...Ke6 3.Kc3 Kd5 4.Kb4.

At move 3
Giving way on the file lets the white king choose a route to the key squares.
If Black played 3...Kc5?, White would reply 4.Kc3 and win. The line would be 3...Kc5 4.Kc3 Kb5 5.Kd4.
If Black played 3...Kc6?, White would reply 4.Kc4 and win. The line would be 3...Kc6 4.Kc4 Kb6 5.Kd5.

At move 4
The defence must keep the barrier in front of the white king; escaping sideways or retreating gives away decisive space.
If Black played 4...Kc6?, White would reply 5.Kc4 and win. The line would be 4...Kc6 5.Kc4 Kb6 6.Kd5.
If Black played 4...Ke4?, White would reply 5.Kc4 and win. The line would be 4...Ke4 5.Kc4 Ke5 6.Kc5.
ex.e11.solution:
1...Ke7! Kings on e1 and e7, five squares between them, White to move: the distant opposition is yours. After 2.Kd2, 2...Kd6!, with three squares between; after 3.Kd3, 3...Kd5!, face to face; and after 4.Kc3, 4...Kc5! The white king never reaches the key squares of the c2-pawn, b4, c4 and d4. Any other first move lets the white king take the opposition, and at every step of the defence only one move holds.

These do not work either:

At move 1: Distant opposition must be obtained on the white king’s file, at the correct distance; a difference of one file or rank opens the approach. If Black played 1...Ke8?, White would reply 2.Kd2 and win. The line would be 1...Ke8 2.Kd2 Kd7 3.Kc3. If Black played 1...Kf7?, White would reply 2.Kd2 and win. The line would be 1...Kf7 2.Kd2 Ke6 3.Kc3.

At move 2: After the change of file, the defence must shorten the distance on the correct axis. If Black played 2...Kd7?, White would reply 3.Kc3 and win. The line would be 2...Kd7 3.Kc3 Kd6 4.Kc4. If Black played 2...Ke6?, White would reply 3.Kc3 and win. The line would be 2...Ke6 3.Kc3 Kd5 4.Kb4.

At move 3: Giving way on the file lets the white king choose a route to the key squares. If Black played 3...Kc5?, White would reply 4.Kc3 and win. The line would be 3...Kc5 4.Kc3 Kb5 5.Kd4. If Black played 3...Kc6?, White would reply 4.Kc4 and win. The line would be 3...Kc6 4.Kc4 Kb6 5.Kd5.

At move 4: The defence must keep the barrier in front of the white king; escaping sideways or retreating gives away decisive space. If Black played 4...Kc6?, White would reply 5.Kc4 and win. The line would be 4...Kc6 5.Kc4 Kb6 6.Kd5. If Black played 4...Ke4?, White would reply 5.Kc4 and win. The line would be 4...Ke4 5.Kc4 Ke5 6.Kc5.
ex.e13: Play White and find the best move. Black has two pawns against one, and the black king threatens to enter along the second rank and capture e3. Keep the pawn protected as the kings change rank.
ex.e13.hint:
Look for a way to reach the black king’s rank without approaching too early. Opposition also works along a rank and from a distance: consider how far apart the kings will be and whose turn it will be.

These do not work either:

At move 1
Approaching before reaching the correct rank lets the black king establish favourable opposition and seek a way in.
If White played 1.Kf2?, Black would reply 1...Kd2 and win. The line would be 1.Kf2 Kd2 2.Kf3 Ke1.
If White played 1.Kf3?, Black would reply 1...Kd1 and win. The line would be 1.Kf3 Kd1 2.Kf2 Kd2.

At move 2
The e3-pawn must be protected while following the black king along the rank. Moving away allows the pawn to be captured immediately.
If White played 2.Kf1?, Black would reply 2...Kxe3 and win. The line would be 2.Kf1 Kxe3 3.Ke1 f4.
If White played 2.Kg2?, Black would reply 2...Kxe3 and win. The line would be 2.Kg2 Kxe3 3.Kf1 f4.

At move 3
The e3-pawn is part of the defence: advancing it gives away a capture and leaves Black with a passed pawn.
If White played 3.e4?, Black would reply 3...dxe4 and win. The line would be 3.e4 dxe4 4.Ke1 e3.
ex.e13.solution:
1.Kg1! Kings on c1 and g1, three squares between them, d1, e1 and f1, and Black to move: the distant opposition along the rank is yours. After 1...Kd2, 2.Kf2!, on the same rank with one square between; after 2...Kd3, 3.Kf3! The black king never sets foot on e2 or e4, and the e3-pawn stays. 1.Kf2? looks more active, but after 1...Kd2 it is your move and Black has the opposition; 2.Kf1? loses to 2...Kd1! {{Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}} shows the same defence, with the pawns one file further right, in example 28 of Chess Fundamentals.

These do not work either:

At move 1: Approaching before reaching the correct rank lets the black king establish favourable opposition and seek a way in. If White played 1.Kf2?, Black would reply 1...Kd2 and win. The line would be 1.Kf2 Kd2 2.Kf3 Ke1. If White played 1.Kf3?, Black would reply 1...Kd1 and win. The line would be 1.Kf3 Kd1 2.Kf2 Kd2.

At move 2: The e3-pawn must be protected while following the black king along the rank. Moving away allows the pawn to be captured immediately. If White played 2.Kf1?, Black would reply 2...Kxe3 and win. The line would be 2.Kf1 Kxe3 3.Ke1 f4. If White played 2.Kg2?, Black would reply 2...Kxe3 and win. The line would be 2.Kg2 Kxe3 3.Kf1 f4.

At move 3: The e3-pawn is part of the defence: advancing it gives away a capture and leaves Black with a passed pawn. If White played 3.e4?, Black would reply 3...dxe4 and win. The line would be 3.e4 dxe4 4.Ke1 e3.
key.lesson: The white king takes the opposition from far away, with several squares between the kings, and closes the gap step by step until it reaches the deciding squares in front of the pawn.
key.capablanca: {{Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}}'s example: locked pawns on both sides and the kings far apart. Whoever is to move takes the distant opposition and wins.
key.carlsenSo: {{Magnus Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}}, playing White, faced {{Wesley So|wesley-so}}, playing Black, at {{Norway Chess|norway-chess}} in {{Stavanger|stavanger}} in 2017. Black was a pawn down and needed to prevent the white king from entering. The black king retreated to obtain distant opposition and followed its opponent from file to file; the game ended in a draw.
key.euweWhitaker: {{Max Euwe|max-euwe}}, playing White, faced {{Norman Whitaker|norman-whitaker}}, playing Black, in The Hague in 1928. The white king obtained distant opposition on the same rank as the black king, approaching the opposing pawn without allowing an equivalent race on the other wing. White won; observe how the kings’ relative positions help reach the target.
history:
Opposition is the contest between kings to force the opponent to give up space; it can begin at a distance or along a diagonal. The goal is to reach an important square, capture a pawn, or prevent an opposing entry. In his 1921 book Chess Fundamentals, {{José Raúl Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}} explains the topic as an author through pawn-ending examples.

The technique also appears in games: at {{Norway Chess|norway-chess}} in {{Stavanger|stavanger}} in 2017, {{Wesley So|wesley-so}}, playing Black, defended an ending a pawn down against {{Magnus Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}}, playing White. The black king followed the white king from a distance, and the game ended in a draw. Just a few pieces can conceal a precise contest for space and time.
practice: Now the real ending: king on h3, pawn on f3 and the black king on e6, eyeing the key squares e5, f5 and g5. Win the opposition on the diagonal, turn it into direct opposition and queen the pawn. Pick your pace and go.
ex.e09.r1: 1...Kf7. The black king leaves the g-file and heads for the centre, towards e6 and d5, in front of the d2-pawn. If the white king does not follow it with the distant opposition on the new file, Black takes it, and the pawn does not get through.
ex.e11.r1: 2.Kd2. The white king changes file, heading for c3 and d3, from where it threatens to reach the key squares of the c2-pawn: b4, c4 and d4. Ask yourself on which square your king keeps the opposition after this change.
ex.e11.r2: 3.Kd3. The white king climbs to the third rank; from d3, one step takes it to c4 or d4, two key squares. There is no room left for the distant opposition: now it has to be direct.
ex.e11.r3: 4.Kc3. The white king tries to outflank along the c-file: from c3, it aims at b4 and c4. If your king does not stand face to face with it, a key square falls.
ex.e13.r1: 1...Kd2. The black king attacks the e3-pawn and looks for a way in through e2. Your king must defend e3 without giving up the opposition along the rank.
ex.e13.r2: 2...Kd3. The black king moves up and attacks e3 from the other side; now the entry it is looking for is e4. The idea is the same: follow it on its rank, with one square between the kings and Black to move.
rot.ideia.ex1.e1: Let's study a basic ending: king and pawn against a lone king.
rot.ideia.ex1.e2: If the pawn runs alone, the black king catches and captures it. Here your king decides.
rot.ideia.ex1.e3: Your king must clear the way for the pawn.
rot.ideia.ex1.e4: To do that, it heads for a key square: once your king gets there, the pawn promotes whatever the black king does.
rot.ideia.ex1.e5: For this pawn, the key squares are f5, g5 and h5.
rot.ideia.ex1.e6: The fight begins: your king wants a key square; the black king wants g6, in front of the pawn, guarding all three.
rot.ideia.ex1.e7: Remember too: the kings can never stand on neighbouring squares. That is why one king shuts the other out.
rot.ideia.ex1.p: White to move. Think and suggest a move, or click {verResposta}
rot.ideia.ex1.certo: Exactly! Your king advances toward the key squares.
rot.ideia.ex1.revela: The best is to advance the king to e4, toward the key squares.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3d4.1: With that move, White no longer wins: Black can draw.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3d4.2: The black king goes to f7, on its way to g6: from there, in front of the pawn, it controls f5, g5 and h5.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3c4.1: With that move, White no longer wins: Black can draw.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3c4.2: The black king goes to f7, on its way to g6: from there, in front of the pawn, it controls f5, g5 and h5.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3e3.1: It looks natural, but with that move White no longer wins.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3e3.2: The black king goes to e7 and faces it, three squares away. Now the opposition belongs to Black.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3c3.1: With that move, White no longer wins: Black can draw.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3c3.2: The black king goes to f7, on its way to g6: from there, in front of the pawn, it controls f5, g5 and h5.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3e2.1: With that move, White no longer wins: Black can draw.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3e2.2: The black king goes to f7, on its way to g6: from there, in front of the pawn, it controls f5, g5 and h5.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3d2.1: With that move, White no longer wins: Black can draw.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3d2.2: The black king goes to f7, on its way to g6: from there, in front of the pawn, it controls f5, g5 and h5.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3c2.1: With that move, White no longer wins: Black can draw.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.d3c2.2: The black king goes to f7, on its way to g6: from there, in front of the pawn, it controls f5, g5 and h5.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.g3g4.1: Pushing the pawn now does not win: Black can draw.
rot.ideia.ex1.err.g3g4.2: The black king runs to f7 and will arrive in time in front of the pawn.
rot.ideia.ex1.livre.fala: Keep playing with White and see how Black defends.
rot.ideia.ex1.livre.volta: Let's go back to the starting position. Suggest another move or click {verResposta}
rot.ideia.ex1.fins.capturado: The black king captured the pawn.
rot.ideia.ex1.fins.repeticao: The black king always closes the way.
rot.ideia.ex1.fins.limite: The black king always closes the way.
rot.ideia.ex1.l1: Notice: your king went to e4, the black king's file. Now there are three empty squares between the kings.
rot.ideia.ex1.l2: When the kings face each other with just one square between them, that is called direct opposition.
rot.ideia.ex1.l3: The side that has just moved has the opposition: now the other king must move and give way.
rot.ideia.ex1.l4: With three squares between the kings, it is the distant opposition: as they close in, it turns into direct opposition.
rot.ideia.ex1.l5: To know who has it, count the empty squares between the kings on the same file or rank.
rot.ideia.ex1.l6: An odd number after your move: the opposition is yours. Here, the king on e4 left three squares: White has it.
rot.ideia.ex1.l7: If it were even, the other king would step up and leave the odd number. So, with each move, leave an odd number.
rot.ideia.ex1.l8: Black has several defences. Let's start with the one that gives White the most trouble.
rot.ideia.ex1.l9: Black brings the king to f7, heading toward the pawn.
rot.ideia.ex1.l10: Their plan is to reach g6 and get in front of the pawn.
rot.ideia.ex1.l11: You get there first: with the king on f5, you face the black king.
rot.ideia.ex1.l12: This is the direct opposition. And f5 is a key square: the black king can no longer reach g6.
rot.ideia.ex1.l13: Why not push the pawn, which looks so natural? The black king would reach g6, in front of it, and shut you out. Watch.
rot.ideia.ex1.l14: Go back one move. Imagine that, instead of taking the king to f5, White pushes the pawn.
rot.ideia.ex1.l15: Black answers with the king on g6, right in front of the pawn. It is the ideal spot for the defense.
rot.ideia.ex1.l16: The white king turns aside to f4, trying to outflank the black king along the f-file.
rot.ideia.ex1.l17: The black king faces it. Now the opposition belongs to Black, and the white king cannot pass.
rot.ideia.ex1.l18: With the white king shut out, White pushes the pawn with check.
rot.ideia.ex1.l19: The black king returns to g6, in front of the pawn, and keeps the way shut.
rot.ideia.ex1.l20: The white king tries to outflank again; the black king steps back and stays in front of the pawn.
rot.ideia.ex1.l21: In the end the black king has no moves, but it is not in check. That is called stalemate, and stalemate is a draw.
rot.ideia.ex1.l22: That is why the king goes first, and the pawn advances only afterwards. Let's go back to the main line.
rot.ideia.ex1.l23: With the king on g7, Black tries again to get in front of the pawn.
rot.ideia.ex1.l24: You follow with the king to g5 and face it again.
rot.ideia.ex1.l25: Another key square taken. Now the pawn advances, protected by the king, and promotes.
rot.ideia.ex1.l26: Now let's go back to the position after the first move.
rot.ideia.ex1.l27: To recap: your king is on e4, with the distant opposition.
rot.ideia.ex1.l28: What if Black defends another way, with the king on e7?
rot.ideia.ex1.l29: You go to e5 and follow the black king, always face to face, to g5, a key square. You know the rest.
rot.ideia.ex1.l34: Back to the starting position. Against other defences the plan holds: win the opposition and reach a key square.
rot.ideia.ex1.l35: Keep the idea: the king goes in front of the pawn and wins the opposition. The pawn only advances afterwards.
rot.ideia.ex1.l36: Now let's look at the defence: how Black uses the opposition to shut the way.
rot.ideia.ex2.e1: Now you play Black, and the board turns around. White has just moved the king to e3.
rot.ideia.ex2.e2: With the right defence, Black holds this position.
rot.ideia.ex2.e4: The white king wants to reach f5, g5 or h5, the pawn's key squares.
rot.ideia.ex2.e5: Your king must shut that path, and the means is the one from the attack: winning the distant opposition.
rot.ideia.ex2.p: Black to move. Think and suggest a move, or click {verResposta}
rot.ideia.ex2.certo: Exactly! Now the distant opposition is yours.
rot.ideia.ex2.revela: The best is to bring the king to e7: the distant opposition now belongs to Black.
rot.ideia.ex2.alt.e8f7.1: Exactly! With the king on f7, Black holds the draw.
rot.ideia.ex2.principal: Your move works too. In the main line, the king goes to e7, on the white king's file, and also wins the distant opposition.
rot.ideia.ex2.err.e8f8.1: This move loses: now White can win.
rot.ideia.ex2.err.e8f8.2: On f4, the white king is on your king's file, three squares apart, with Black to move: the distant opposition is his.
rot.ideia.ex2.err.e8d8.1: This move loses: now White can win.
rot.ideia.ex2.err.e8d8.2: The white king goes to f4, next to f5 and g5: from d8, your king cannot get there in time to control them.
rot.ideia.ex2.err.e8d7.1: This move loses: now White can win.
rot.ideia.ex2.err.e8d7.2: The white king goes to f4, next to f5 and g5: from d7, your king cannot get there in time to control them.
rot.ideia.ex2.livre.fala: Keep playing with Black and see how White attacks.
rot.ideia.ex2.livre.volta: Let's go back to the starting position. Suggest another move or click {verResposta}
rot.ideia.ex2.fins.coroa: The pawn promoted. Without the opposition, Black cannot hold.
rot.ideia.ex2.fins.limite: The white king controls the key squares: the pawn will promote.
rot.ideia.ex2.fins.repeticao: The white king controls the key squares: the pawn will promote.
rot.ideia.ex2.fins.capturado: The pawn fell: your king won the fight for the key squares, and it is a draw.
rot.ideia.ex2.fins.afogado: The black king was stalemated: stalemate is a draw, and the defence held.
rot.ideia.ex2.l1: Three squares between the kings, odd, and you have just moved: the opposition is yours; White must give way.
rot.ideia.ex2.l2: White has several tries. Let's start with the most direct one.
rot.ideia.ex2.l3: White advances the king through the center.
rot.ideia.ex2.l4: You answer by facing it, on e6: direct opposition.
rot.ideia.ex2.l5: The white king turns aside to f4, trying to outflank your king along the f-file.
rot.ideia.ex2.l6: Your king follows to f6 and faces it again: direct opposition.
rot.ideia.ex2.l7: With no way through for the white king, White pushes the pawn.
rot.ideia.ex2.l8: Your king goes to g6, in front of the pawn: the ideal spot for the defense.
rot.ideia.ex2.l9: The white king reaches no key square. It is a draw.
rot.ideia.ex2.l10: Now let's go back to the position with your king on e7.
rot.ideia.ex2.l11: What if, instead of seeking the opposition, the white king turns aside to f4 to outflank you along the f-file?
rot.ideia.ex2.l12: You face it again, on f6. The opposition is still yours.
rot.ideia.ex2.l13: And what if, instead of stepping up to f6, your king goes to f7, near g8, the promotion square, to defend from behind?
rot.ideia.ex2.l14: That gives up the opposition: the white king, already on f4, reaches f5, a key square, first, and the pawn promotes.
rot.ideia.ex2.l15: White takes advantage: the king goes to f5, takes a key square and faces the black king. The pawn will promote.
rot.ideia.ex2.l16: That is why, against the king on f4, the answer is f6: facing it, keeping the opposition.
rot.ideia.ex2.l17: Back to the position with your king on e7. In defence, whoever holds the opposition shuts off the key squares.
rot.ideia.ex2.l18: Win the opposition and bring the king in front of the pawn.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.1: First position: the pawn is one rank further back, on the second rank.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.2: Since the pawn is one rank further back, the key squares are one rank further back too: f4, g4 and h4.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.25: The rule: the key squares are the square two ranks in front of the pawn and its two neighbours.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.25b: It holds for pawns on the b- to g-files. The edge pawn, on a or h, follows another rule, seen in another lesson.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.26: With the pawn on b3, for example, the key squares would be a5, b5 and c5.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.3: Your king steps up to e3, on the same file as the black king.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.4: Count the squares between the kings: three, an odd number, and you have just moved. The distant opposition is yours.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.5: Black heads for the pawn with the king on f7.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.6: Your king reaches f4, which is already a key square.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.7: Black goes to g6 and stands in front of the pawn.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.8: You stand face to face on g4: direct opposition, on a key square.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.9: That is the winning move: you keep the opposition, and the black king has to step aside.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.10: The black king runs to the corner, and your king stays ahead of the pawn all the way to g6.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.16: Let's go back to the starting position.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.17: What if White pushes the pawn at once, two squares, to g4?
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.18: With the pawn on g4, the key squares move up with it, to f6, g6 and h6, and the black king is one step from f6.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.19: Black brings the king to f6 and guards the key squares.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.20: The white king comes to help, but it is far from the key squares f6, g6 and h6.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.21: The black king attacks the pawn and stands in front of it.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.22: White can only defend the pawn. The black king never leaves its path: it is a draw.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.23: Let's go back to the starting position.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.24: With the pawn further back, the key squares move back too. The king leads with the opposition; the pawn follows.
rot.demos.tempo.1: Second position: the same as before, now from Black's side, and the board has turned.
rot.demos.tempo.2: Only the move has changed. If Black has the move in this position, Black can organize a draw.
rot.demos.tempo.29: When having the move decides who gets the opposition, we say that side has the tempo.
rot.demos.tempo.24: How? By advancing the king to take the opposition before the white king, then standing before the pawn.
rot.demos.tempo.3: Your king steps forward to e6, toward the pawn's key squares.
rot.demos.tempo.4: From here your king can always answer with the opposition. Going to f6 also holds: it also nears the key squares.
rot.demos.tempo.5: White uses the attacking plan: the king goes to e3.
rot.demos.tempo.25: Count: two squares between the kings, even. Step forward and leave one: odd, and the opposition is yours.
rot.demos.tempo.6: You face it on e5. One square between the kings, an odd number, and you have just moved: the opposition is yours.
rot.demos.tempo.7: From here it is the defence of the second example: if the white king tries to outflank, yours stays facing it.
rot.demos.tempo.15: With the opposition, your king guards the key squares and the white king cannot get through: it is a draw.
rot.demos.tempo.26: Let's go back to the starting position.
rot.demos.tempo.27: What if Black moves the king to d6, on the white king's file?
rot.demos.tempo.28: Three squares between the kings, and Black has just moved: the distant opposition is theirs. It also holds.
rot.demos.tempo.30: Notice: the black king went to the white king's file, as your king did in the attacking example, going to e4.
rot.demos.tempo.31: Kings on different files? Bring yours to the other's file and leave an odd number of squares: the opposition is yours.
rot.demos.tempo.16: Let's go back to the starting position.
rot.demos.tempo.17: What if Black moves the king to f7, heading toward the pawn?
rot.demos.tempo.18: Here going to f7 loses: with the pawn on g2, f4 is already a key square, and the white king gets there in two moves.
rot.demos.tempo.19: White takes advantage: the king goes to e3.
rot.demos.tempo.20: Black hurries to g6, in front of the pawn.
rot.demos.tempo.21: Too late: the white king reaches f4, a key square, and the pawn will promote.
rot.demos.tempo.22: Let's go back to the starting position.
rot.demos.tempo.23: Same position, opposite results: whoever moves first leaves the odd number, keeps the opposition and decides the ending.
rot.demos.erroAtacante.1: Third position, from Black's side: White moved the king to e2, not to e3.
rot.demos.erroAtacante.2: It looks almost the same, but count the squares between the kings: now there are four.
rot.demos.erroAtacante.3: An even number: White has miscounted. Step forward and leave an odd number: the opposition is yours.
rot.demos.erroAtacante.4: Your king advances to e6. Now there are three squares between the kings, an odd number, and you have just moved.
rot.demos.erroAtacante.5: The distant opposition is yours. Stepping to f6 also holds; any other move hands it back to White.
rot.demos.erroAtacante.7: You stand face to face on e5. It is the same position we saw a moment ago, and it is a draw.
rot.demos.erroAtacante.14: Count the squares between the kings. If your opponent left an even number, step up and take the opposition.
rot.pratica.ataque.enunciado: Play White and find the best move.
rot.pratica.ataque.fim: Your king led the way with the distant opposition, and the pawn advanced only afterwards.
rot.pratica.ataque.err.f3e3.1: With 1.Ke3?, your king goes to the black king's file but leaves four squares between them: the win slips away.
rot.pratica.ataque.err.f3e3.2: Even: the opposition is Black's. After 1...Kd7, if 2.Kd4, 2...Kd6! takes the direct opposition and guards c5.
rot.pratica.ataque.err.f3f4.1: With 1.Kf4?, your king advances off the black king's file and does not win the distant opposition: the win slips away.
rot.pratica.ataque.err.f3f4.2: 1...Kd7! and, next move, 2...Kc6: the black king gets beside b5 and c5 before yours.
rot.pratica.ataque.err.f3g4.1: With 1.Kg4?, your king moves away from the pawn and from the key squares a5, b5 and c5: the win slips away.
rot.pratica.ataque.err.f3g4.2: 1...Kd7! and, next move, 2...Kc6: the black king gets beside b5 and c5 before yours.
rot.pratica.ataque.err.f3g3.1: With 1.Kg3?, your king moves away from the pawn and from the key squares a5, b5 and c5: the win slips away.
rot.pratica.ataque.err.f3g3.2: 1...Kd7! and, next move, 2...Kc6: the black king gets beside b5 and c5 before yours.
rot.pratica.ataque.err.f3g2.1: With 1.Kg2?, your king retreats, away from the pawn and from the key squares a5, b5 and c5: the win slips away.
rot.pratica.ataque.err.f3g2.2: 1...Kd7! and, next move, 2...Kc6: the black king gets beside b5 and c5 before yours.
rot.pratica.ataque.err.f3f2.1: With 1.Kf2?, your king retreats and loses time racing to the key squares a5, b5 and c5: the win slips away.
rot.pratica.ataque.err.f3f2.2: 1...Kd7! and, next move, 2...Kc6: the black king gets beside b5 and c5 before yours.
rot.pratica.ataque.err.f3e2.1: With 1.Ke2?, your king keeps the distant opposition but retreats too far and is late for b5 and c5: the win slips away.
rot.pratica.ataque.err.f3e2.2: 1...Kd7! If 2.Kd3, 2...Kc7! holds; the natural 2...Kc6? would lose to 3.Kc4!, with the direct opposition.
rot.pratica.ataque.err.b3b4.1: With 1.b4?, the pawn moves before the king, and the key squares move up to a6, b6 and c6: the win slips away.
rot.pratica.ataque.err.b3b4.2: 1...Kd7! The black king is already beside c6, and your king, on f3, is far from the new key squares.
rot.pratica.defesa.enunciado: Play Black and find the best move.
rot.pratica.defesa.fim: Your king took the distant opposition in time and did not let the white king through.
rot.pratica.defesa.err.b7c7.1: With 1...Kc7?, your king reaches the white king's file with four squares between them: the draw slips away.
rot.pratica.defesa.err.b7c7.2: An even number: the opposition belongs to White. After 2.Kd3 Kd6 3.Kd4 Ke6, 4.Ke4! wins the direct opposition.
rot.pratica.defesa.err.b7b6.1: With 1...Kb6?, your king leaves the white king's file and does not win the distant opposition: the draw slips away.
rot.pratica.defesa.err.b7b6.2: 2.Kd3 Kb5 3.Ke4! The white king gets beside f4, a key square, and yours, on b5, is far from the pawn.
rot.pratica.defesa.err.b7b8.1: With 1...Kb8?, your king retreats away from the pawn and does not win the distant opposition: the draw slips away.
rot.pratica.defesa.err.b7b8.2: 2.Kd3 Kb7 3.Ke4! The white king gets beside f4, a key square, with no fight for the opposition.
rot.pratica.defesa.err.b7c8.1: With 1...Kc8?, your king has the distant opposition but retreats too far and is late to the pawn: the draw slips away.
rot.pratica.defesa.err.b7c8.2: 2.Kd2 Kd7 3.Ke3 Ke6 4.Ke4! The white king gets beside f4 first and wins the direct opposition.
rot.pratica.defesa.err.b7a8.1: With 1...Ka8?, your king moves away from the pawn and leaves its square: the draw slips away.
rot.pratica.defesa.err.b7a8.2: 2.g4! The pawn advances two squares and runs to g8, and your king, on a8, cannot catch it.
rot.pratica.defesa.err.b7a7.1: With 1...Ka7?, your king moves away from the pawn and leaves its square: the draw slips away.
rot.pratica.defesa.err.b7a7.2: 2.g4! The pawn advances two squares and runs to g8, and your king, on a7, cannot catch it.
rot.pratica.defesa.err.b7a6.1: With 1...Ka6?, your king moves away from the pawn and leaves its square: the draw slips away.
rot.pratica.defesa.err.b7a6.2: 2.g4! The pawn advances two squares and runs to g8, and your king, on a6, cannot catch it.
rot.ideia.ex1.l6b: Why? If the black king steps forward, two squares remain; yours steps too, one remains, and he must give way.
rot.ideia.ex1.l20b: The pawn reaches g7, but the black king is still on g8, in front of it.
rot.ideia.ex2.ponte: I play both sides in three positions now. See who wins the opposition and if the attacker gets a key square.
rot.demos.fileiraAbaixo.10b: Only now does the pawn advance, protected by the king, and promote.
rot.demos.erroAtacante.ponte: Your turn: one attack and one defence against the machine. Before each move, count the squares between the kings.
title: Distant opposition
summary: Taking the opposition from afar, with an odd number of squares between the kings, to reach the key squares, protect the pawn and keep the enemy king out.
ex.e18: Play as White and find the best move. The pawns are locked on c5 and c6 and the black king guards the rear. Find the route of your king to the enemy pawn.
ex.e18.hint: Your king should not go straight at the black king: go around it along a file it cannot reach and arrive from behind.
ex.e18.solution: 1.Kf6! starts to go around the black king. After 1...Kd7, 2.Kf7! passes through a square the black king cannot reach. After 2...Kd8, 3.Ke6! squeezes the black king, and 3...Kc7 allows 4.Ke7! It is Black to move and any king move gives way, so the white king ends up capturing the c6 pawn.
ex.e18.r1: 1...Kd7. The black king steps out to d7 and guards e6 and c7, trying to stop the white king from entering along the e-file.
ex.e18.r2: 2...Kd8. The black king steps back to d8, trying to cover e8 and e7.
ex.e18.r3: 3...Kc7. The black king returns to c7 to protect the c6 pawn.
ex.e19: Play as White and find the best move. The a-file pawns are locked and the black king is more active. Your king must reach the other side in time.
ex.e19.hint: It is a race: your king must go to meet the black king through the centre, without losing time, to get counterplay.
ex.e19.solution: 1.Kd7! starts the race against the black king. After 1...Kc5, 2.Ke6! heads for the centre; after 2...Kc4, 3.Ke5! and, after 3...Kc3, 4.Ke4! Your king arrives in time to defend and to attack the enemy pawn, and the draw is secured.
ex.e19.r1: 1...Kc5. The black king rushes to the centre and to the side of the a-file pawns.
ex.e19.r2: 2...Kc4. The black king drops another rank, threatening to enter on the queenside.
ex.e19.r3: 3...Kc3. The black king reaches c3 and threatens to go to b2 to attack the a2 pawn.
coach.allPartsDone: Now you know how to win the opposition and take your king to the key squares. Shall we go to the final test?
part.means.title: Choose the target
part.means.summary: Taking the opposition is not the goal: if your king can reach one of the pawn’s key squares directly, go there, even without the opposition.
key.means: The opposition is a means, not the goal: here taking it only draws. What wins is taking the king straight to the deciding squares in front of the pawn.
